lines.text: Right into the catcher mitt. Well folks, welcome in to American Family Field for Game One of the World Series. Forty-three thousand, two hundred and fifty folks settled in under the roof with sixty-nine degree comfort, and nobody has a victory in this ledger yet. Nick Martinez is ready on the mound for Tampa Bay, and our own Jacob Misiorowski is toeing the rubber for Milwaukee. Gabe Morales has the indicator behind the plate. Let us play ball.

That roof overhead is keeping things at sixty-nine degrees here at American Family Field, and forty-three thousand, two hundred and fifty of us are snug as three bugs in a rug. Nick Martinez, the thirty-six-year-old right-hander from Miami they call Tricky, is getting his glove set. And our twenty-four-year-old from Blue Springs, Jacob Misiorowski, stands six-foot-seven on that mound, looking like he could catch a falling star without even reaching up. Gabe Morales has the plate.
Ball one, count's 1 and 0. Yandy Díaz, Aranita, stepping into it like he’s got the rhythm of a Cuban salsa line. Misiorowski’s got that steady arm, just waiting for the next one.
Ball one, count’s 1 and 0. Four-seamer out of the zone, Díaz swings and the ball jumps back—hard enough to make the count 1 and 1. That one came in like a neighbor’s dog barking at the mailman.
Misiorowski deals the hundred-miler, Díaz lifts it deep toward right, Frelick tracks it near the line, chases it down, and hauls it in for the first out. Score remains tied at zero.
I never could hit a curveball, but Josh Stutting has never met a tech problem he couldn't send to the bleachers. Reach him at stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.

Jonathan Aranda steps in, 28 years old, from Tijuana, standing six feet nothing, first base, looks like he’s trying to stay out of the way. Misiorowski fires a four-seam, 103, called strike. Count’s now 0 and 1.

Four-seam fastball, 103, foul tip — count's now 0 and 2. Aranda's trying to stay light on the heels, but Misiorowski's arm's been steady since the first pitch. That one bounced like a kid's shoe on a concrete step.
Aranda’s got a good stance, but Misiorowski’s got that four-seamer on repeat—like a tape loop in a basement heater. Keep eyes on the line, first base’s a quiet spot.

Aranda's got that bat in his hands, swings it like a man with a key to a locked door, and the ball pops out—line drive, 171 feet, right field. Frelick's got it in the air, eyes locked, and it's gone. One out, runners on first. Still tied at zero.
Misiorowski’s got that four-seamer on repeat, just like the old heater in the basement—six pitches so far, all fast, all straight, and still no one’s cracked a smile at the plate.

Misiorowski fires a four-seam, 102, ball — count's now 1 and 0. Simpson's got that long frame, but he's not known for stretching. That one rolled in like a slow truck on a country road. One out, runners on first, still tied at zero.

Runners on first, one out, count now 1 and 1. Misiorowski fires a four-seam, 101, foul — that one slipped past the glove like a neighbor’s dog at dusk. Simpson’s got that long frame, but he’s not known for stretching. The ball just hung there like a phone call you didn’t want to answer.

The ball slapped the plate like a tired cat on a cold porch, swinging right through the zone. Count's now 1 and 2. Simpson's got that long frame, but he’s not known for stretching. Misiorowski’s got that four-seamer on repeat—like a tape loop in a basement heater.

Misiorowski’s got that four-seamer on repeat—like a tape loop in a basement heater—and the series hasn’t even started, so it’s already feelin’ like we’re in the middle of a slow march down a dark hallway.
Count's now 1 and 2. Misiorowski fires a four-seam, 103, foul — that one slid past the glove like a flashlight in the back of a barn at 3 a.m. Runners on first, one out, still tied at zero.

The ball skipped off the infield like a coin tossed in a coffee cup — just one runner moving, no rally yet, but Simpson’s got that long frame, and you know what they say about long frames and quiet starts.

Chandler Simpson pokes an eighty-eight mile per hour curveball softly out to left, resting safely on a single while Jonathan Aranda trots up to second base, leaving runners on first and second with one out, still scoreless here in the first.
Simpson’s got that long frame, and he’s been at the plate since the series started—just like a car that’s been parked in the driveway for weeks, waiting for the first key turn.

Caminero meets Misiorowski’s four-seam at 102, it stays low and just hovers over the plate like a porch light in a drafty house — ball, count's now 1 and 0. Runners on first and second, one out, still tied at zero.

Misiorowski brings that ninety-six mile per hour cutter right over the heart of the plate to Caminero, and he taps it softly right to the hot corner Hamilton snatches it on the fly, fires over to second to double them up and get us out of the jam, and that side is retired with no damage done, still scoreless here in the top of the first!

That brings the top of the first to a close with nobody crossing the plate and two hits for Tampa Bay. Still scoreless here. Folks, before our crew arrived, Milwaukee cheered for the Braves, champions back in fifty-seven. Let us see what our boys can do.
I never made it out of the minors, but you don't have to wait on a call-up. Northcentral Technical College in Wausau is ready when you are. Look up Northcentral Technical College at N T C dot edu.

Forty-three thousand two hundred fifty folks settled into American Family Field tonight under sixty-nine degree closed roof comfort, watching Jacob Misiorowski work with eleven four-seam fastballs so far.

Martinez deals a ninety-one mile per hour cutter to Chourio, and he pounces on it, sending it on a line out to right field. Chourio pokes that eighty-five mile per hour liner just over the grass for a clean single, and the Brewers have their first baserunner of the night, still scoreless!

First baseman Bauers steps into the box, and Martinez tries a pickoff, fingers flicking across the plate—JB just barely keeps his feet, and that’s the only thing the count knows for now. Still, zero balls, zero strikes.

Martinez fires a ninety-one mile per hour cutter, ball, making it 1-0. Bauers stays ready, that’s the only thing we’ve got going here. Tricky’s got a fastball in his back pocket, but it’s not quite his best.

Jake Bauers takes the mound, Martinez fires a 95 mile per hour sinker, it lands just over the plate, called strike. Count now stands at one ball, one strike. Bauers stays steady, fingers twitching, trying to find the rhythm.
Slider from Martinez, just inside, called strike. Count now 1-2. Bauers stays poised, eyes locked on the plate. That one slipped past his glove like a late-night snack he forgot to eat.
A tip of the cap to Josh Stutting, the wizard who keeps this booth on the air. Your business could use a wizard too. stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.

Martinez winds up slow, fingers dancing near the glove, sends a 92-mile-per-hour cutter that curls just outside—ball, count now 2 and 2. Bauers stays square, eyes fixed, waiting for the next move. That one didn’t quite find the edge of the plate, but it sure had the look of one that might’ve been aimed at a forgotten mitt.

Runners on first, count at 2 and 2, Bauers swings at a four-seam fastball, 95 miles per hour, foul line. Ball stays down, no change. Still no one on base, just a long pause in the air, like a dropped mitt at dusk.
Bauers’ got that first-base gap to watch for, especially if the ball sneaks in low — Martinez hasn’t got much variety, just that cutter, so the infield’s gonna be feeling it.
Bauers lifts a fly ball to right fielder Victor Mesa Junior, and Victor squeezes it for the first out. Still no score here in the first.
Count’s dead even, first pitch of the at-bat, and Martinez hasn’t thrown a single fastball yet—just that one cutter, like he’s trying to find a parking spot in a garage full of ghosts.

Slider 86, called strike, count's now 0 and 1. Yelich, big guy with a patient eye, waits for the next one. Martinez’s got that cutter in his pocket, but hasn’t shown it yet. First pitch, first move—still building the rhythm.

Four-seam fastball, 95 miles per hour, swinging strike. Count’s now 0 and 2. Yelich stands there, calm as ever, waiting for the next one. Martinez’s got that cutter tucked in, but he’s starting with a straight line.

Ball drops to the foul line, just shy of the wall, 78 miles per hour, changeup. No change. Count’s now 0 and 2. Yelich stands there, eyes steady, waiting for the next one. Martinez’s got that cutter tucked in, but he’s starting with a straight line.
One out, men on first, Yelich’s got patience like a man waiting for the bus—Martinez’s got that cutter in his glove, but he’s still trying to find the right corner to drop it in.
Martinez comes in with that sinker, 94, down the pipe, foul. Count’s still 0 and 2. Yelich stays put, like he’s waiting for the moon to rise. That one didn’t make the cut, but it sure as heck tried.
Yelich’s been waiting for that one, and Martinez’s got three cutters in his glove—like he’s trying to find a parking spot in a garage full of ghosts. Still no runs, just rhythm.

Yelich digs in again with two strikes, Martinez deals that cutter at ninety-one, Christian catches it just right and drives it deep into the center field grass. He laced that one a hundred and three miles an hour, and it sails all the way to the wall for a triple! Chourio races home from first, and the Brewers are on the board first, leading one to nothing!

Martinez deals that ninety-one mile per hour cutter right over, Contreras swings and connects hard there it goes, a sharp line drive at one hundred eight miles an hour off the bat, deflected by shortstop Walls into left field, Christian scores, and the Brewers add another to lead two to zero!
Mound visit, just like we’ve seen before. Turang stays calm, ready to go.

Turang takes a look at that 94-mile-an-hour sinker, swings and misses, foul pop. Count's now 0 and 1. One out, runners on first, Brewers up 2 to 0. Martinez's got that pitch in his glove, just waiting for the right moment to drop it.

Slider 85, foul, count’s now 0 and 2. Turang stays back, just waiting. Martinez’s got that slider in his glove, like he’s trying to find a parking spot in a garage full of ghosts. One out, runners on first, Brewers up 2 to 0.

Martinez fires that ninety-four mile an hour four-seam fastball, and it misses the mark. One ball and two strikes now to Brice Turang, with one out and runners on first in the bottom of the first, Brewers leading two to nothing.

Into the dirt and blocked. Turang swings through that seventy-eight mile an hour changeup and down he goes. Two outs now in the first, runners still on first, and the Brewers hold a two to nothing lead.
First game, no winners yet, and Turang’s got a fresh bat, just like the first time he stepped into a lineup—no pressure, just a chance to show what he’s made of.

Garrett Mitchell swings at that 86-mile-an-hour slider, foul it goes, count’s now 0 and 1. Two out, runners on first, Brewers up 2 to 0. Mitchell’s been hitting .207 this post season, got two homers in eight games, but this one’s just a little off the plate.

Changeup, Turang swings and misses, foul tip, count's now 0 and 2. Two out, runners on first, Brewers up 2 to 0. Mitchell's been working the count, but this one just slipped through like a sock in the laundry.
Martinez sets up, hands in the glove, eyes on the plate. That four-seam, 94, cuts in from the mound, foul it goes. Count's now 0 and 2. Two out, runners on first, Brewers up 2 to 0.

Changeup drops in the dirt, soft as a Sunday morning nap, making it 1 and 2. Mitchell stays on the plate, eyes locked, just waiting for the next one. Still two outs, runners on first, Brewers leading 2 to 0.

Martinez comes in, hands in the glove, eyes on the plate. That changeup, 79, floats just over the plate, ball. Count's now 2 and 2. Mitchell stays on the plate, just waiting. Two out, runners on first, Brewers up 2 to 0.
Runners on first, two out, Martinez fires that 94-mile-an-hour sinker, ball, count’s now 3 and 2. Mitchell stays in the zone, eyes fixed, just waiting for the next one. Brewers lead 2 to 0.

Full count now on Mitchell. Martinez deals that seventy-seven mile an hour changeup, he swings and misses, and that will do it for the first inning here in Milwaukee. Three outs now, bases empty, and our Brewers still lead it two to zero.

Right into the catcher's mitt that half inning comes to a close. Two runs on three hits for Milwaukee, and we head to the second with our boys on top two to zero. Robin Yount sure knew how to move around, taking home two MVPs at two different spots. Let's see what the Rays can cook up now.
A word from Josh Stutting. Gandalf had his staff, Merlin had his beard, and Josh has the wifi password. He'll get you connected. stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.
Mitchell stepping out of the on-deck circle now, twenty-eight years old from Orange, California, carrying two postseason home runs into the box.

Nine-nine fastball, strike. Count's now 0 and 1. Hicks stands there, eyes locked, just waiting. Misiorowski fires that one down the middle, smooth as a Sunday morning drive. Still nothing on the board, just the silence between pitches.

Ball dives down the third base line, just shy of the bag, foul pop. Count's now 0 and 2. Hicks, 27, from Toronto, stands there, hands tucked in, eyes steady. That cutter at 97, tight as a belt loop. Nothing on the board yet.

Turang fields that one cleanly, tosses on over to Bauers for the out. Sixty-eight mile an hour grounder, that trickled slower than my old Buick on a frosty January morning. One away now, bases empty, Brewers still lead it two to zero.
Hicks, 27, from Toronto, stepped into the box for the first time in the postseason, and I’ve never seen a rookie catcher so calm — like he’s been here before, even if he hasn’t.

Four-seam fastball, called strike. Count's now 0 and 1. DeLuca, 28, from Thousand Oaks, steps up, looks ready to go, but this one didn’t quite find the sweet spot. Just a solid one, like a well-worn shoe on a Tuesday morning.
Ninety-mile-per-hour slider, that misses down and away. Count moves to one ball and one strike now on DeLuca, bases empty, one out, top of the second inning, Brewers still out in front two to zero.

Misiorowski deals another one-hundred-one-mile-per-hour fastball, DeLuca lifts that high into the afternoon sky, carrying it out to center where Mitchell settles underneath and squeezes it. That stayed up in the air longer than my grandmother's Thanksgiving biscuits. Two down now, Brewers still lead two to zero.
Bases are empty, count's dead even, and Misiorowski’s got those fastballs working like a well-oiled machine—first pitch, no rush, just waiting to see what DeLuca’s got.

Count's now 0 and 1. Mesa, 25, from Havana, Cuba, steps up with a look like he’s just learned how to swing — no pressure, just pure instinct. Misiorowski fires that four-seam at 99, straight and true, strikes it clean.
Misiorowski’s got 19 pitches on the board tonight, all four-seamers so far, like he’s trying to keep the game on a steady road—no curves, no cutters, just a straight line from the mound to the plate.

Misiorowski brings that four-seam fastball right down broadway at one hundred and one miles per hour, called strike. Count is now zero and two, bases empty, two out here in the top of the second inning, Brewers leading two to nothing.

Mesa’s got that Cuban fire in him, and he’s not afraid to take the long route to the outfield—DeLuca’s in center, Walls down in the corner, and if that ball goes deep, they’ll have to watch for the wind.

Mesa steps in facing Misiorowski, zero and two, nineteen pitches in, and that ninety-eight mile per hour cutter comes in diving with some real mustard on it he chases it and misses the air entirely for strike three, and that side is finally retired here in the second with the Brewers still holding a two to nothing lead

That closes out the top of the second inning with zero runs and zero hits for Tampa Bay, leaving our score at two to zero in favor of Milwaukee, hits now standing at two for the Rays and three for our crew. Way back in nineteen seventy-five and seventy-six, Hank Aaron finished his legendary career right here in town playing his final two seasons in a Brewers uniform. Let us take a short breather and see what the bottom of the second brings us.
Not everybody makes the big club, but everybody can build a great career, and Northcentral Technical College in Wausau is a fine place to start. Northcentral Technical College, N T C dot edu.
Forty-three thousand two hundred and fifty folks settled in here under the roof tonight, watching game one of this series unfold inside American Family Field.

Out to left field goes Chandler Simpson, settling right underneath that eighty-nine mile per hour fly ball from Cooper Pratt, and Simpson squeezes it for the first out here in the bottom of the second, score remaining Milwaukee two, Tampa Bay zero.
Yelich’s triple in the first went like a well-timed delivery—straight to DeLuca, and Chourio just rolled in like he’d been waiting all season.

Frelick takes the plate, count at zero and one, that slider from Martinez dipped just enough to make the plate, quiet as a Sunday morning, no flash, just a touch of edge. He’s got a .200 clip in this series so far, but that doesn’t mean much yet.
Count at one and one, Sal Frelick looks at that 93 mile per hour sinker from Martinez, the ball just hovers over the plate, no flash, no fire—quiet as a Tuesday morning, stays clean and tight.

Martinez delivers an eighty-five mile per hour slider for a called strike, then misses with a ninety-three mile per hour sinker, and on one and one comes the seventy-eight mile per hour changeup Frelick stays back and pokes that eighty-six mile per hour ground ball right through the right side into the outfield for a clean single, and the Brewers keep the line moving with one away and a man on first, still holding that two to zero lead.

Martinez deals that eighty-four mile per hour slider, Hamilton drops down a bunt, rolls to the mound, Martinez underhand tosses to Williamson for the out as Frelick takes second, two away now in the second, Milwaukee two, Tampa Bay zero.
Fun fact: Josh Stutting's tech fixes have a better batting average than the entire nineteen eighty-two Brewers lineup. Okay, I made that up, but it feels true. stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.
Sinker at 94, ball, count now 1 and 0. Chourio waits, just like he did in the first inning, steady as a porch swing on a cool day. Martinez keeps it clean, no flash, just a touch of edge.

Chourio waits, just like he did in the first inning, steady as a porch swing on a cool day. Sinker at 94, foul tip, count now 1 and 1. That one didn’t break much, just skimmed the outside corner, like he’s trying to find his rhythm in the heat of the moment.

Chourio stays back on that 79 mile per hour changeup, just shy of the inside edge, the ball curls a little like a tired old porch swing, count now 2 and 1, two out, runner on second, Brewers still hold that two to zero lead.
Chourio waits on that ninety-one mile per hour cutter, takes it low and away for ball three. Count now three balls and one strike, two away, runner on second, Milwaukee leading two to zero.
Chourio’s got that first-time look, 22 years old, from Maracaibo, and he’s 1 for 1 tonight—still trying to find the rhythm, like a rookie learning how to ride a bike without training wheels.

Sinker at 95, swinging strike, count now 3 and 2. Chourio stays back, just like he did in the first inning, steady as a porch swing on a cool day. Two out, runners on second, Brewers still hold that two to zero lead.

Martinez’s got those changeups working, eight of them so far, like he’s trying to sneak them past the fence on a quiet night—still no strikeout, but the rhythm’s coming in slow and steady, like a porch light turning on after dark.
Jackson Chourio comes up with the count at 3 balls, 2 strikes. Sal Frelick sprints to third, steals it clean.
Martinez checks the sign, fires that ninety-five-mile-per-hour sinker, Chourio swings through it for strike three Oh no, he got him! He went fishing in the dirt and the inning is over!

That wraps up the second inning with zero runs on one hit for Milwaukee, and we still hold a two to zero lead over Tampa Bay. The Rays got their start back in nineteen ninety-eight as the Devil Rays and made it to the big series in two thousand eight and two thousand twenty. Let us see what the third brings us.
Josh Stutting: turning 'it's broken' into 'it's working' since before it was cool. stutting dot josh at gmail dot com. That's s, t, u, t, t, i, n, g, dot, j, o, s, h, at gmail dot com.
That roof overhead is shut tight keeping things at sixty-nine degrees here inside American Family Field where forty-three thousand two hundred fifty folks have packed the place.

Ben Williamson takes a look at that four-seam, 99 mph fastball, lets it roll past him, and it’s a ball. Count’s now 1 and 0. Misiorowski’s got that pace, but Williamson’s just holding steady, like he’s waiting for the next one to find its rhythm.

Ben Williamson looks at that four-seam, 101 mph fastball, lets it roll past him, and it’s a strike. Count’s now 1 and 1. Misiorowski’s got that pace, but Williamson’s just holding steady, like he’s waiting for the next one to find its rhythm.

Williamson takes that 100 mph four-seamer, lets it slide by, and it’s a strike. Count’s now 1 and 2. Misiorowski’s got a fresh rhythm, but Williamson’s just standing there, like he’s waiting for the next one to decide whether it’s worth chasing.

With the count at 1 and 2, Williamson faces Misiorowski’s 103 mph four-seam, swings at it, and it clips the outside corner—foul. Still 1 ball, 2 strikes. Williamson’s holding steady, waiting for the next one to settle in.
Slider 90 mph, slips by Williamson just shy of the plate, lands in the dirt. Count’s now 2 and 2. He’s got a good feel for the pitch, but that one slipped through like a sock in a dryer.

Misiorowski fires that 92 mph slider, it curls just inside the plate, and it’s a ball. Count’s now 3 and 2. Williamson’s looking steady, like he’s waiting for the next pitch to decide whether it’s going to be a walk or a fight.

Misiorowski comes right back with a hundred-one-mile-per-hour heater, Williamson rolls it down toward first, Bauers takes it himself and steps on the bag for the out. That grounder crawled slower than my catching career. One away here in the third.
Count’s dead even, bases empty, and Misiorowski’s got a fastball that’s been a little slower lately—still sharp, still sharp, just not quite the thunder I remember from his first start.

Taylor Walls takes that 101 mph four-seam, lets it roll just past the plate—ball. Count’s now 1 and 0. Misiorowski’s got a fresh arm, but Walls’s got a calm look, like he’s thinking about where the next one might go.

Walls takes that 102 mph four-seam, swings at it, and it’s a strike. Count’s now 1 and 1. He’s got a solid eye, though he’s not had much luck this postseason, just 4 hits in 27 tries. Still, he’s standing tall, like he’s got a plan.
Walls stays back on the rubber, looks at the curveball, 89 mph, and swings — strike. Count’s now 1 and 2. He’s got a steady hand, but that one dipped in like a spoon in cold milk.

Misiorowski brings that ninety-five-mile-per-hour cutter, Walls reaches out and tips it foul. Count stays one and two here in the third, Brewers holding a two to nothing lead while Jacob goes back to work.
Walls’s got a .148 clip this postseason, and he’s been in the box 27 times without a homer—like a slow burner trying to light a candle in a drafty basement.

Walls looks at that 89 mph slider, swings at it, and it clips the outside corner—foul. Count’s still 1 and 2. He’s been patient through it, but that one dipped in like a spoon in cold milk. Still, he’s standing tall.

Walls lets that four-seam roll just past the plate—ball. Count’s now 2 and 2. He’s been patient through it, but that one slipped in like a spoon in cold milk. Still standing tall, like he’s waiting for the next one to decide what to do.

Misiorowski looks in, deals that cutter, and Walls stands frozen as the umpire rings him up on the outside corner Strike three and he is gone, Jacob paints the black and leaves him standing there with the bat on his shoulder, two away now in the third and the Brewers still holding that two to nothing lead

Four-seam fastball, 102 mph, foul — count’s now 0 and 1. Díaz, Aranita, stands tall, looking for his first crack at the plate tonight. Just one for the season so far, but he’s been hot since the opener, like a well-oiled machine finding its rhythm.

Slider coming in at ninety-three miles per hour, Díaz lines that one sharply out to second, right to Turang who makes the snag for out number three. That rocket left at one hundred two miles per hour and still the Brewers lead two to nothing.

That takes care of the top half, and Misiorowski keeps our boys ahead two to nothing with four hits to their two. Reminds me, that nineteen eighty-two series with St. Louis was called the Suds Series, and we lost in seven. Let us see what the bottom of the third brings.

If your fastball tops out at fifty, like mine did, maybe technology, health care, or the trades are more your speed. Northcentral Technical College in Wausau can get you there. That's Northcentral Technical College, N T C dot edu.
Forty-three thousand two hundred fifty souls are packed inside American Family Field beneath a closed roof with the mercury sitting at sixty-nine degrees for this series opener.
Martinez fires that slider, 85, foul, count's now 0 and 1. Tricky, he's been a little slow lately, but still sharp. Bauers stands there, eyes fixed, waiting for the next one.

The ball drops soft to the dirt, just past first base, count's now 1 and 1. Bauers stands there, calm, waiting for the next one. Martinez's fastball, 95, just shy of his usual pace, rolled in with a quiet hum.

Martinez fires a changeup, 79, tight and just a touch too slow, called strike. Count's now 1 and 2. Bauers stays rooted, eyes on the plate, waiting for the next one. Still a little slow lately, but never stopped being sharp.

Bauers takes the pitch, swings at the four-seam fastball at 94, makes contact, the ball drops soft to the dirt just past first, count's now 2 and 2. He's been patient, steady, that one didn't go in a bigger hurry than I ever did.

The slider drops just outside, 85, foul, count still dead even. Bauers stands there, calm, eyes locked on the plate. Martinez's slider, a little bit late, like he's trying to catch up with his own shadow. Still sharp, though, just a touch slow on the timing.

Martinez deals that changeup at seventy-eight, Bauers swings and misses, and that's down on strikes, one away now here in the bottom of the third, Brewers still holding a two to nothing lead over the Rays.
A word from our sponsor, and frankly our only sponsor, Josh Stutting. When your computer throws you a curveball, Josh hits it into the upper deck. stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.

Martinez starts with a 94-mph sinker, clean and crisp, right on the edge of the strike zone, called strike. Count's now 0 and 1. Yelich, 34, stands tall, calm, like he’s seen this before—just one strike, one more to go.
Martinez comes back with an eighty-five-mile-an-hour slider, missed the outside corner, and that evens the count at one and one. Yelich stays locked in right there in the home dugout's backyard.
Martinez slips that changeup just inside, 78, soft, the glove barely brushes the dirt. Count's now 2 and 1. Yelich stays in, eyes on the plate, like he's waiting for the next one to settle.
Count’s even, one out, Yelich due up, and look at that — Martinez’s changeups are dropping like leaves in October, just shy of the ground, but still got enough bite to make the dirt tremble.
Martinez brings that cutter at ninety-one, Yelich swings through it. Count moves to two and two now.
Martinez’s last ten pitches have dipped to 87, just like the old porch light in winter — steady, maybe a little dimmer, but still holding its own.
Martinez lets it go, four-seam, 94, just outside the corner, foul. Count still sits at 2 and 2. Yelich doesn’t flinch, stands square, like he knows this one’s not going to be easy.
Martinez tries the eighty-five-mile-an-hour slider, misses wide outside, and that fills the bucket at three and two. Yelich remains locked in, standing tall in the home dugout neighborhood.

Yelich swings at the cutter, foul, count stays 3 and 2. Still on the edge of that plate, like he’s waiting for the next one to settle. Martinez’s got a few more to go, but the count’s stuck where it is.
One out, bases empty, count’s 3-2, Yelich’s got that triple from the first, and Martinez’s last ten pitches have dipped to 87 — just like the porch light when the wind starts to pick up.
Martinez goes back to the four-seam fastball at ninety-four, Yelich swings and misses for the third out. Two gone now in the third, and our boys still lead it two to nothing.

Yelich cracked that triple like he’d been waiting all season — sharp, clean, right into DeLuca’s hands — and that’s how we got those first two runs, just like he did in ‘13 when he first stepped into the lineup.

That four-seam fastball at 94, foul, just outside the corner, count now 0 and 1. Contreras, 28, from Puerto Cabello, stands ready, hasn’t swung yet, but you can feel the quiet hum in the air like a radio tuned just off the dial. Still got that .367 to work with.

Mesa Jr takes two steps in and squeezes it in right. That sinker at ninety-five got the job done, and that does it for the third. Three innings in the books, and our boys still lead it two to nothing.

That closes out the third, with our boys still holding a two to nothing lead on four hits to their two. Before we turn to the fourth, remember Christian Yelich took home the National League MVP award back in eighteen. Let us see what the fourth brings us.
Josh Stutting: he builds it, he fixes it, he teaches it, and he still finds time to root for the Brewers. stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.
Forty-three thousand two hundred fifty folks settled into American Family Field tonight under sixty-nine degrees with the roof closed, watching Martinez throw his fifty-first pitch.
